title: Should Musicians Use AI? A Recent Music School Grad Asks

content: Getty Images Little Miss AI is a recurring advice column. Have a question? Email us! Q: I recently graduated from a renowned music school. Do you think I should work on adopting the technology and incorporating it into my own work as a musician, engineer, and general professional, or should I avoid and/or resist its use as much as possible and develop my skills without the assistance of AI? Which do you think looks better to an employer in the music industry? And do you think that answer will change as AI improves? — Aaron S., Natick A: Thank God for the artists, am I right? Poets, painters, actors, singers, and dancers light up our lives in a uniquely human way. At least for now. Aaron, the questions you ask are fair and prescient. They touch upon concerns that all of us, in just about every industry, are raising, too. I spoke to a few people in the music world who could offer some guidance. My first call was to Jonathan Wyner , a musician, performer, producer, and engineer who has mastered and produced more than 5,000 recordings over the past 40 years with artists such as James Taylor, David Bowie, Aerosmith, Miles Davis, Thelonious Monk, Pink Floyd, Bruce Springsteen, and Nirvana. You might expect him to be a musical purist, but he is not. He’s currently the director of Berklee College of Music’s Emerging Artistic Technology Lab (BEATL), where his job is to assist educators, artists, and industry leaders with engaging in AI. He is open and supportive of integrating AI into a musical career. “Artists at the center is our credo and our goal,” he says. “We are trying to help musicians understand where the opportunities are, and how to make smart decisions.” Image generated in Perplexity by Lisa Pierpont. That begins with gaining a deep knowledge of composition, harmony, culture, and live performance. That’s non-negotiable. Rather than fearing displacement in performance or trying to compete with pure AI generation, Wyner says musicians should leverage AI for business infrastructure, tour management, artist management, and corporate media production. And while he considers AI-generated music to be technically competent—convincing enough for background music or corporate applications—it rarely moves audiences the way a live human performance does. He also makes the significant point that currently, AI-generated music lacks copyright protection, meaning uploading third-party audio could violate rights. Next, I chatted with Daniel Pfeiffer, a live mix and sound engineer with the Boston Landmarks Orchestra and Wingbeats Recording Studio on Cape Cod . He feels adamantly that AI is not equipped (at least right now) with the same tools that humans possess. “There are so many dimensions to music beyond what meets the ear. Humans sense and communicate in ways that go far deeper than musical construction, timbre, and balance,” he says. “AI cannot replace the human—and, I would argue, divine—act of musical creativity.” That said, Pfeiffer appreciates that resisting technology would be like a modern contractor refusing to use power tools. For young music students, he advises making as little use of AI as possible during the foundational years: “Learn and grow to be a creator.” However, the minute you land a job, leverage it. “Use it for efficiency and value to career advancement.” Finally, I strongly encourage you to check out relevant local events to get a sense of where things are going in the future. Be sure to add the annual AI Music Summit , hosted by BEATL, to your calendar. Based at the Hilton Boston Back Bay, the program is open to the public (details here ). Also keep an eye out for the Boston Symphony Orchestra’s “Technology and Our Humanity” initiative. The BSO recently commissioned and premiered the symphony Already and Not Yet by Tod Machover . Conducted by Kent Nagano, the work blended an MIT Media Lab–designed AI system that performed and improvised in real time alongside BSO musicians. Future programs include panel discussions and AI audio projects at Symphony Hall and MIT. For upcoming events, visit bso.org . To view recent performances, check out the BSO NOW streaming platform and the MIT Media Lab event archive . Aaron, I look forward to hearing how your career progresses. Whether you’re plucking strings across a wooden violin or prototyping a song through AI, may music forever bring you joy and fulfillment. Previously: Should I Trust LLMs with My Medical Data?
